With Eq. 35, we have:

𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(σS)\displaystyle\mathsf{Goodput}(\sigma_{S}) ≥δ1+δ⋅∑U∈σSR⁡(U)\displaystyle\geq\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\sum_{U\in\sigma_{S}}R(U) (37)
=δ1+δ⋅∑U∈σS∑V∈σ∗f⁡(U,V)\displaystyle=\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\sum_{U\in\sigma_{S}}\sum_{V\in\sigma_{*}}f(U,V) (38)
=δ1+δ⋅∑V∈σ∗∑U∈σSf⁡(U,V)\displaystyle=\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\sum_{V\in\sigma_{*}}\sum_{U\in\sigma_{S}}f(U,V) (39)

Combining with the per-request bound Eq. 32, we have:

𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(σS)\displaystyle\mathsf{Goodput}(\sigma_{S}) ≥δ1+δ⋅𝔄⁡(δ,α,β,γ)⋅∑V∈σ∗R⁡(V)\displaystyle\geq\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\mathfrak{A}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\cdot\sum_{V\in\sigma_{*}}R(V) (40)
=δ1+δ⋅𝔄⁡(δ,α,β,γ)⋅𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(σ∗)\displaystyle=\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\mathfrak{A}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\cdot\mathsf{Goodput}(\sigma_{*}) (41)

where

𝔄⁡(δ,α,β,γ)=min⁡(α,α1+δ,β,β1+δ,γ⋅(1+δ)3)\mathfrak{A}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\;=\;\min\Bigl(\alpha,\,\frac{\alpha}{1+\delta},\,\beta,\,\frac{\beta}{1+\delta},\,\gamma\cdot(1+\delta)^{3}\Bigr) (42)

Therefore, we can conclude that there exists a constant competitive ratio for JITServe:

𝔅⁡(δ,α,β,γ)=δ1+δ⋅min⁡(α1+δ,β1+δ,γ⋅(1+δ)3)\mathfrak{B}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\;=\;\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\min\Bigl(\frac{\alpha}{1+\delta},\frac{\beta}{1+\delta},\,\gamma\cdot(1+\delta)^{3}\Bigr) (43)
Optimize objective function.

It is clear that the maximum lower bound can be achieved by optimizing over δ,α,β,γ\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma under the constraints δ>0\delta>0, α≥0,β≥0,γ≥0\alpha\geq 0,\beta\geq 0,\gamma\geq 0, and α+β+γ≤1\alpha+\beta+\gamma\leq 1, i.e., formally, we need to solve the optimization problem to attain the maximum competitive ratio:

maxδ,α,β,γ\displaystyle\max_{\delta,\,\alpha,\,\beta,\,\gamma}\quad 𝔅⁡(δ,α,β,γ)\displaystyle\mathfrak{B}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma) (44)
𝗌.𝗍.\displaystyle\mathsf{s.t.}\quad α+β+γ≤1\displaystyle\alpha+\beta+\gamma\leq 1 (45)
α≥0,β≥0,γ≥0\displaystyle\alpha\geq 0,\,\beta\geq 0,\gamma\geq 0 (46)
δ>0\displaystyle\delta>0 (47)

Solving these above optimization problem using numerical analysis [18] yields an optimal performance guarantee of JITServe r′​(δ)≈18.13r^{\prime}(\delta)\approx\frac{1}{8.13}. Note that as we discussed in Section 4, preemption can improve the performance of our online algorithm JITServe, but it also introduces practical overhead. Figure 23 illustrates the trade-off between preemption overhead and the competitive ratio: the xx-axis is the preemption threshold δ\delta, and the yy-axis is the performance guarantee of JITServe. To balance objective maximization and implementation overhead, we choose a moderate threshold of δ=10%\delta=10\%, which slightly relaxes the bound yet yields a performance guarantee that remains acceptable in practice.

Theorem D.3 (Constant competitiveness of JITServe with GMAX).

The scheduling of JITServe with GMAX is constant competitive when compared with the optimal oracle scheduler: there exists r>0r>0 such that

𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(J​I​T​S​e​r​v​e)𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(OPT)≥r\frac{\mathsf{Goodput}(JITServe)}{\mathsf{Goodput}(\mathrm{OPT})}\;\geq\;r (48)
Proof.

We now continue from the above lemma to complete the proof. Note that we now have already had a performance guarantee for our JITServe scheduling algorighm under no-GMAX scenario. We are now ready to prove that our JITServe scheduling together with GMAX also has a performance guarantee.

Top-pp Filtering

We are now ready to prove that GMAX will only introduce a uniform (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-loss surrogate for each served request. Fix any batching decision time. Let R⁡(r⁡(b))R(r(b)) denote the bb-th largest goodput value among all currently available requests. By the GMAX rule, the candidate set is

𝒯:={W:R⁡(W)≥p⋅R⁡(r⁡(b))}.\mathcal{T}:=\{W:\ R(W)\geq p\cdot R(r(b))\}. (49)

Consider any request UU that σS\sigma_{S} would serve (or continue to serve) at this time. Because σS\sigma_{S} maintains batch size bb, necessarily R⁡(U)≥R⁡(r⁡(b))R(U)\geq R(r(b)). Hence there exists some U′∈𝒯U^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T} with

R⁡(U′)≥p​R​(r⁡(b))≥p​R​(U).R(U^{\prime})\ \geq\ p\,R(r(b))\ \geq\ p\,R(U). (50)

Intuitively, U′U^{\prime} is a surrogate for UU that is always almost as valuable in terms of its goodput value; the length adjacency constraint in GMAX only determines which bb requests inside 𝒯\mathcal{T} are taken, but it never drives any selected R⁡(⋅)R(\cdot) below the threshold p⋅R⁡(r⁡(b))p\cdot R(r(b)). Therefore, replacing UU by U′U^{\prime} in any lower-bound argument causes at most a multiplicative pp degradation.

Putting together.

Combining Eq. 43 from Lemma 1 and Eq. 50, we now have

𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(σS)≥p⋅δ1+δ⋅𝔅⁡(δ,α,β,γ)⋅𝖦𝗈𝗈𝖽𝗉𝗎𝗍⁡(σ∗)\mathsf{Goodput}(\sigma_{S})\geq\frac{p\cdot\delta}{1+\delta}\cdot\mathfrak{B}(\delta,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\cdot\mathsf{Goodput}(\sigma_{*}) (51)

Solving these above optimization problem using numerical analysis [18] under our experimental setting yields an optimal performance guarantee of JITServe r⁡(δ)≈18.557r(\delta)\approx\frac{1}{8.557}.
